title: Google's ATLAS v1.0 maps 15M Gemini conversations to 800 occupations — full automation under 10%
subtitle: The first data-anchored study of AI usage in the U.S. economy shows Gemini reaches 68% of occupations, but end-to-end task automation remains rare and collaboration dominates.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google published ATLAS v1.0 — the 'AI & Economy Activity, Task, Landscape, and Adoption Study' — on July 23. It is built on 15 million de-identified interactions across the Gemini App, Google AI Mode and the Gemini API, mapped to 800 occupations, 4,000 tasks, 300 household activities, 150 countries and 140 languages. The headline finding: AI adoption reaches 68% of occupations covering roughly 90% of U.S. employment, but fewer than 10% of interactions represent attempts at end-to-end task automation. The remaining 90% cluster around collaboration, ideation, drafting, retrieval and learning.

The mechanism worth naming is the collaboration ratio. In routine cognitive work — data entry, straightforward summarization, form-filling — automation intent runs above 25%. In non-routine cognitive work — strategy, negotiation, complex writing — it stays under 10%, even among heavy users. That gap is what distinguishes ATLAS from earlier academic 'labor exposure' studies that projected job replacement percentages. Those studies asked what tasks a model could do; ATLAS observed what people actually asked it to do. The gap between capability and delegation turns out to be large, and it is the single most important variable for near-term labor-market impact.

The study also lands in the middle of a live policy fight. The Congressional Budget Office and the White House have both cited pre-AI labor exposure estimates to model displacement risk, and those estimates ranged from 10% to 40% of hours automatable. ATLAS's under-10%-actual-automation finding, from the largest single dataset published to date, will complicate any policy grounded in the higher-end projections. Expect this paper to be cited in every AI-labor debate over the next year, on both sides — its underlying data supports both 'AI is complementing workers, not replacing them' and 'we are barely a year into serious agentic capability, wait.'

For learners: capability is not deployment. A model that could do your job in a controlled benchmark is not the same as a model your employer would trust to do it unsupervised. That trust gap — legal, cultural and technical — is the thing that determines whether AI advances your career or ends it. The learners who benefit most from AI over the next five years will be the ones who become the human in the loop for the tasks their team is trying to automate, not the ones who resist automation and not the ones who over-trust it.
